scores.evidence: A failover can lose a few seconds of counter increments. We accept that: it briefly weakens velocity features and doesn't block authorisations.
scores.rationale: Claims about Redis cluster hash-tag atomicity, ONNX/LightGBM parity, Kinesis per-key ordering, at-least-once dedup and fail-open stand-in semantics are all accurate, and real limits (failover loss, duplicate in-flight) are stated rather than glossed.

scores.evidence: this plan assumes you are a card issuer deciding on your own cardholders' authorisations
scores.rationale: It resolves the request's biggest ambiguity explicitly, covers inline scoring, rules, labels, review and retraining, and defers step-up, graph and multi-region with stated triggers; the 5-person team scope is credible.

scores.evidence: Velocity counters ctr:{c:…} | Redis (derived, rebuildable) | Decision Service | Atomic per card via Lua
scores.rationale: Single-writer-per-key-prefix, system-of-record tables, consistent fail-open policy and the readiness-check-vs-degraded reasoning show one coherent design with no contradictions found.

scores.evidence: Four spikes answer the processor contract, data/label availability, Redis hot-path latency, and model-scoring parity.
scores.rationale: The riskiest assumptions are tested in week 1–4 spikes with explicit 'changes plan if' conditions, targets are labelled provisional [A8], and validation continues in production via shadow, cohort control, reconciliation and PSI drift.

scores.evidence: I picked defaults and labelled each one [A#]; they're all listed in Section 5.
scores.rationale: Every design-bearing assumption is explicit with impact-if-wrong and a validation step, numbers are marked as estimates, and sensitivity (10× scale, Python-only team, PAN in payload) is spelled out.

scores.evidence: If it holds a stored decision, we return it without incrementing anything. If it is still 'pending' ... we compute a read-only decision.
scores.rationale: Covers duplicates, Redis failover, Kinesis loss, deadline misses, mass false declines, counter-probing, label poisoning and insider tampering with concrete detection/containment/recovery; only reversal counter-correction detail is thin.

scores.evidence: on-call is 24/7 from M3 (the first enforcement). That needs at least 4 people on the rotation
scores.rationale: Deployment, sub-minute rollback paths, Flyway expand/contract migrations, named alerts with thresholds, runbooks and an ownership split between fraud ops and engineering are all sized to the stated team.

scores.evidence: The real cost drivers are people and false declines. Controls: AWS Budgets alerts at 80% and 100%
scores.rationale: Run costs are ranged with a stated scale basis, the dominant drivers are correctly identified as people and false declines, controls are concrete, and build-vs-buy (D0) is reasoned on cost.

scores.evidence: Point of no return: effectively none while the processor's rules remain. It arrives when processor-side rules are retired
scores.rationale: Each key decision carries a reversibility rating and revisit trigger, the language choice is flagged as the hard one-way door with an alternative, and schema/feature versioning keeps persisted formats additive.

scores.evidence: avoids learning and running Flink (5-person team), and is atomic per card
scores.rationale: Deliberately rejects Flink, a feature-store product and microservices with stated reasons, while a deferred-work table gives explicit triggers to add each later; nothing essential is cut.

scores.evidence: Changes plan if: deadline < 100 ms (co-locate, drop the merchant call); no inline hook (switch to post-authorisation design)
scores.rationale: T0–T10 tasks have 'done when' criteria, the critical path and long-lead items are called out for day 1, and each spike states how disappointing results change the plan.

checklist.evidence: Server-side p99 ≤ 50 ms at 500 TPS ... hard deadline 120 ms, then fallback
Redis exceeds 15 ms or its circuit breaker is open: switch to degraded mode ... Fail open.
Training features come from replaying history through the same feature code used online ... prevents training/serving skew by construction
Chargebacks arrive 30–90+ days late ... joins them to labels that are at least 120 days mature ... on a time-split holdout
value detection rate at 0.3% decline vs. the rule baseline ... Present the M2 baseline as a curve of fraud caught vs. decline rate
Actions: APPROVE, DECLINE, APPROVE_REVIEW ... Rules as CEL expressions in Git, hot-loaded via signed artefact + AppConfig
Analysts label cases, manage lists, and trigger cardholder notifications ... Label Joiner (consumes analyst labels from Case Service)
No PAN anywhere [A7] ... With the PAN, the adapter enters PCI scope ... and must tokenise on entry
card.lua finds idem:<auth_id>. If it holds a stored decision, we return it without incrementing anything ... Partition key is the card token
Shadow first, then cohort ramp ... score PSI (population stability index, a drift measure) > 0.2 vs. the training distribution
100% of decisions logged with a feature snapshot and versions ... rule_hits[] (id, mode, action), ruleset_version, model_version, score
peak 500 TPS ... load test at 1,000 TPS (2× peak) ... Multi-AZ throughout, and at least 3 Decision Service tasks

traps.evidence: Inline synchronous decisioning in one service, with the model running in-process (ONNX Runtime)
120 ms overall deadline, 15 ms Redis timeout + circuit breaker ... decide on rules alone
evaluates it against the champion on the last 8 matured weeks ... PR-AUC, and value detection rate ... on a time-split holdout
a 1,000-event replay produces identical counts in the Redis and in-memory store implementations
No PAN anywhere [A7] ... Logs carry auth_id only, never the token

note: An exceptionally strong, internally consistent plan: inline sub-50ms scoring with explicit degraded/fail-open policy, skew-free training by construction, early spikes on the riskiest unknowns, and proportionate scope; only reversal counter handling and dollarized people costs are marginally thin.
